clue.text: Cab heading off to the centre of Rome? It's taken for granted

definitions.note: a clause standing for a noun: an axiom is a thing taken for granted

indicators.note: the cab's heading, its first letter, comes off
only the two middle letters of Rome are wanted

blocks.note: TAXI without its first letter T
the middle two letters of rOMe

explanation.surface: A tourist assumes a taxi will take them straight to the heart of Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: Rome has four letters, so its centre is the middle pair, OM.
explanation.definitionFit: An axiom is a statement accepted as true without proof, something taken for granted.

clue.text: Bad sex tour I'm organising, having no first-hand experience!

definitions.note: the adjective phrase stands for the adjective

indicators.note: organising the letters puts them into a new order

explanation.surface: A cheeky jibe at someone arranging a seedy holiday they have never been on themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a pun: it reads as inexperience, but means no first hand, since neither hand comes first for an ambidextrous person.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone ambidextrous uses both hands equally well, so has no first, or dominant, hand.

clue.text: Going ahead with home loan

blocks.note: an advance is a loan of money

explanation.surface: A couple pressing on with a mortgage to buy a house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Home loan' reads as a mortgage; it splits into two words that each give a piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym used adverbially: something done ahead of time, like booking ahead, is done beforehand.

clue.text: Award for boy brought up by Orlando

indicators.note: in a down clue, bringing a word up makes it read bottom to top

blocks.note: Orlando is the setter, so the setter's name stands for ME

explanation.surface: A prize for a child raised by a man called Orlando.
explanation.walkthrough: Orlando is this puzzle's setter, and a setter naming themselves means ME. 'By' puts ME beside the reversed boy.
explanation.definitionFit: A medal is the metal disc handed out as a prize for bravery, service or winning, so a specific kind of award.

clue.text: Max may be associated with this space for nuts

definitions.text: Max may be associated with this
definitions.note: a clause pointing at the word, not a synonym

blocks.clueFragment: Max may be associated with this
blocks.note: Max is the first name of a 1980s computer-generated TV presenter; this is his surname
nut is slang for head, so room for heads

explanation.walkthrough: Max Headroom was a 1980s computer-generated TV presenter, so Max goes with HEADROOM. Nut is slang for head, so space for nuts is room for heads.
explanation.definitionFit: Headroom is the clear space above your head.

clue.text: Makes bequests with no difficulty at all

blocks.note: to hand down is to pass on to heirs
an idiom for an easy win, from a jockey so far ahead he can drop his hands and the reins

explanation.walkthrough: The two meanings sound unrelated: to hand down is to leave to your heirs, and winning hands down is winning easily.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who hands down possessions makes bequests; 'hands down' also means with ease.

clue.text: Primate holding first of services in church recess

indicators.note: the primate holds the letter inside it
only the first letter of services is taken

explanation.surface: A monkey clutching a hymn sheet in a church alcove at the start of a service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Primate' can also mean a senior archbishop, which fits the church picture, but here it is just an ape.
explanation.definitionFit: An apse is a semicircular recess, usually at the east end of a church.

clue.text: Show trial?

blocks.note: the surface reads a staged political show trial; really it is a theatre show
not a court case but a trial run of the show

explanation.walkthrough: A show trial is a staged political prosecution; read differently, it is a trial run of a show.
explanation.definitionFit: A rehearsal is a practice performance, a trial of a show before it opens.

clue.text: Old and useless like an egg

blocks.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A stale egg, past its best and good for nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like an egg' is the definition, an adjective phrase matching OVOID, so the egg is not the thing described as old.
explanation.definitionFit: From Latin ovum, egg: ovoid describes the oval, one-end-fatter shape of an egg.

clue.text: Does it teach children how to get on?

definitions.text: Does it teach children how to get on?

blocks.note: the surface points to any school
the surface reads 'succeed in life'; really it means to board, get on a vehicle

explanation.walkthrough: 'Get on' suggests getting on in life; the pun is getting on board, as if boarding were the subject taught.
explanation.definitionFit: A boarding school is one where pupils live during term, and to board is to get on.

clue.text: Running nude in street, not giving a hoot

indicators.note: running letters are set loose from their order

explanation.surface: A streaker dashing down the road without a care for who is watching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Running' reads as a streaker's jog, but it is the instruction to rearrange the next three words.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: a hoot is a tiny amount, so someone who does not give a hoot has no interest at all.

clue.text: Attractive person concealing wickedness is diabolical

indicators.note: the attractive person hides the wickedness inside

blocks.note: a dish is slang for an attractive person

explanation.surface: A charmer hiding a wicked streak is truly fiendish.
explanation.walkthrough: A dish is British slang for an attractive person.
explanation.definitionFit: Devilish means like the devil, diabolical.

clue.text: Virgin soldiers accepting assistance?

indicators.note: the soldiers take the assistance in among them

blocks.note: men = soldiers, as in officers and men

explanation.surface: Raw recruits needing help, a nod to the novel and film The Virgin Soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Virgin soldiers' reads as one phrase, but Virgin alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A maiden is a virgin; as an adjective, maiden also means untried.

clue.text: Phone box designed by European who fears foreigners?

definitions.note: a relative clause standing for the noun 'one who fears foreigners'

indicators.note: letters designed anew are rearranged

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: The red British telephone box, pictured as the work of an insular European.
explanation.walkthrough: 'European' looks like part of the person being defined, but it only supplies the E.
explanation.definitionFit: Built from Greek xenos, stranger, and phobos, fear, so the word itself spells out the definition.

clue.text: Bill has upset French king? The American ass!

definitions.note: American 'ass' means backside; POSTERIOR is the noun

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset turns the word upside down, so it reads upward

blocks.note: a bill is a poster, as in 'stick no bills'

explanation.surface: Someone called Bill has offended a French monarch, and is branded a fool of an American.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ass' looks like an insult for a fool; with 'The American' it means backside.
explanation.definitionFit: In American English ass means buttocks, and posterior is a polite word for the buttocks.

clue.text: Listen secretly, hearing of woman's fall

indicators.note: what we hear is the sound of the phrase, not its spelling

blocks.note: Eve is a woman's name and a drop is a fall

explanation.surface: Overhearing gossip about a woman taking a tumble.
explanation.walkthrough: Eve, the first woman, had the original Fall, which makes the woman's fall a neat pun.
explanation.definitionFit: Originally someone standing under the eaves, where rainwater dripped, to overhear what was said inside.

clue.text: Country beginning to suffer distress

indicators.note: the beginning of suffer is its first letter

explanation.surface: A nation starting to fall on hard times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beginning to' takes only the first letter of suffer; the rest of that word plays no part.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Spain is one of many possible countries, so the crossing letters matter.

clue.text: One setting out unto a star?

definitions.text: One setting out unto a star?

indicators.note: the letters are set out in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A space traveller heading off towards a distant star.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: someone setting out for a star is an astronaut, and the question mark flags the double reading.
explanation.definitionFit: An astronaut travels into space, literally a star sailor.

clue.text: Revolvers smuggled in somewhere else

indicators.note: the answer is carried secretly inside the next words

explanation.surface: Handguns being slipped illegally into another country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolvers' wants to be guns; here it means things that revolve.
explanation.definitionFit: A reel is a spool that revolves, so reels are revolvers.

clue.text: Written work takes half a month and then correspondence is incomplete

indicators.note: half of the month's name is dropped
the correspondence is missing its last letter

explanation.surface: A writer spends a fortnight on a piece while their letters go unfinished.
explanation.walkthrough: Half a month is not NOV, the usual abbreviation, but half of the eight letters of NOVEMBER.
explanation.definitionFit: A diminutive of novel, so a short piece of fiction, one kind of written work.

clue.text: No longer bound to get involved in duet

indicators.note: letters that get involved are tangled together

explanation.surface: A singer freed from a contract so they can take part in a duet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a linking word, but it is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: knots or ropes that bound something have been undone, leaving it free.

clue.text: Belief not affected by reversal

indicators.note: a word unchanged when turned round reads the same both ways

blocks.note: no letters from the words themselves: the answer must read the same in both directions

explanation.surface: A conviction that holds firm even after a setback.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives no letters, only a property: find a word for belief that reads the same in both directions.
explanation.definitionFit: From Latin 'he holds': a doctrine or principle that someone holds to be true.

clue.text: Get away, having swallowed half of loaf or slice of meat

indicators.note: the escape takes the letters inside it
only the first half of loaf is kept

explanation.surface: A thief escapes having wolfed down bread or a bit of meat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Or' is a link word: the definition is the slice of meat, while the loaf only lends two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An escalope is a thin slice of boneless meat, often veal.

clue.text: Beheading a clergyman is a serious crime

indicators.note: the head, the first letter, is cut off the clergyman

blocks.note: PARSON without its first letter P

explanation.surface: Executing a vicar would indeed be a grave offence.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a true statement, which hides that beheading is an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Arson, deliberately setting fire to property, is a serious crime.

clue.text: Last pieces of Henry Moore and Barbara Hepworth? Sure!

indicators.note: the last piece of each name is its final letter

explanation.surface: Asked whether the final works of two great British sculptors count as masterpieces, someone agrees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pieces' suggests sculptures, which fits two sculptors; 'and' is skipped, and only the four names give letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are casual spoken ways of agreeing; the exclamation mark marks it as an interjection.

clue.text: What may be prescribed to remedy tenant's despair

definitions.note: a clause standing for a noun

indicators.note: remedying the letters means putting them right, into a new order

explanation.surface: A doctor treating a renter's misery with medication.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as the definition, which is fitting, but only the first four words define and the despair is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: An antidepressant is a drug a doctor may prescribe.

clue.text: Enterprise, perhaps, making celebs groovy

explanation.surface: A business venture that makes famous people look cool.
explanation.walkthrough: Enterprise looks like a business; it is the starship Enterprise from Star Trek, and 'perhaps' flags it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example, flagged by 'perhaps': the USS Enterprise is the famous spacecraft of Star Trek.

clue.text: Marked absence of Edward?

blocks.note: absence of something is not having it: NOT

explanation.surface: Edward's non-attendance was recorded.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark signals that 'absence of' is read literally, as the word NOT placed before Edward's short form.
explanation.definitionFit: Noted means observed or marked, as in 'marked his absence'.
